subject: obstetrics-gynaecology
title: Endometrial carcinoma: Bokhman dual pathogenesis, Lynch syndrome and FIGO staging

steps.tx: Endometrial carcinoma is the most common gynaecological malignancy in developed nations. Clinically, over ninety percent of affected women present early with **postmenopausal bleeding**. In postmenopausal patients presenting with abnormal spotting, transvaginal ultrasound measurement of the endometrial stripe provides high negative predictive value. A stripe thickness exceeding four millimeters mandates histological confirmation via outpatient Pipelle biopsy.
steps.say: Endometrial cancer is the most common gynaecological cancer, presenting with postmenopausal bleeding in over ninety percent of cases. An endometrial thickness over four millimeters on ultrasound requires prompt biopsy to exclude cancer.

steps.tx: The classical clinicopathological classification described by Bokhman separates endometrial cancer into two distinct biological categories. **Type I endometrioid carcinoma** represents eighty percent of cases, occurs in perimenopausal women, is driven by unopposed estrogen and obesity, arises from atypical hyperplasia, and harbors PTEN and microsatellite instability mutations. In contrast, **Type II serous carcinoma** is estrogen-independent, arises in atrophic endometrium, carries TP53 mutations, and has poor prognosis.
steps.say: The Bokhman classification divides endometrial cancer into two types. Type one is estrogen-driven, linked to obesity, and has a favorable prognosis. Type two comprises serous and clear cell tumors arising in older women with TP53 mutations and aggressive behavior.

left.title: Type I Endometrioid Carcinoma
points: Accounts for 80% of cases, diagnosed in perimenopause
Driven by chronic unopposed estrogen and obesity
Mutations: PTEN (80%), PIK3CA, KRAS, ARID1A, MSI-H

right.title: Type II Serous / Clear Cell Carcinoma
points: Accounts for 10-20% of cases, older postmenopausal women
Estrogen-independent, arises in thin atrophic uterus
Aggressive, early peritoneal spread, poor prognosis

steps.tx: All newly diagnosed endometrial carcinomas require screening for **Lynch syndrome** (hereditary non-polyposis colorectal cancer). Caused by germline mutations in DNA mismatch repair genes (MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, PMS2), Lynch syndrome confers a lifetime endometrial cancer risk of forty to sixty percent, equal to or exceeding the lifetime risk of colorectal cancer in affected women. Universal reflex immunohistochemical testing identifies families requiring genetic counseling.
steps.say: All endometrial cancers should be screened for Lynch syndrome. Caused by mismatch repair mutations, it confers a forty to sixty percent lifetime risk of endometrial cancer. Universal immunohistochemistry identifies affected families for genetic testing.

steps.tx: Staging of endometrial cancer follows the **FIGO surgical staging system** performed via minimally invasive total laparoscopic hysterectomy, bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy, and sentinel lymph node mapping. Stage I is confined to the uterine corpus, subdivided by myometrial invasion depth into Stage IA (less than fifty percent) and Stage IB (fifty percent or greater). Stage II invades cervical stroma, Stage III demonstrates locoregional spread, and Stage IV invades bladder, bowel, or distant organs.
steps.say: Endometrial cancer is staged surgically with laparoscopic hysterectomy, removal of ovaries, and sentinel node mapping. Stage one is limited to the uterine body, stage two invades the cervix, stage three extends into the pelvis or lymph nodes, and stage four involves distant organs.

rows: Confined to endometrium or < 50% myometrial invasion
Observation (or vaginal vault brachytherapy if G3)
Invasion into cervical stromal connective tissue
Invasion of bladder/bowel mucosa (IVA) or distant organ (IVB)
